n: Religious experts travel all the way from Jerusalem to Galilee to investigate Jesus — a sign that the leaders are watching him closely.
They accuse Jesus’s disciples of skipping the ritual hand-washing before meals. This was about ceremonial purity, not hygiene.

f.g: Oral rules handed down by earlier rabbis, meant to “fence” the law of Moses; later written in the Mishnah.

n: Jesus turns the question around: their traditions actually break God’s commandments.

f.g: transgress = break, step over a boundary.

n: He cites the Ten Commandments: honor your parents. The law treated cursing parents as a capital crime.
Their tradition let a person declare property a “gift” dedicated to God, so it couldn’t be used to support aging parents.

f.g: Mark uses the Hebrew term Corban — something vowed to God.

n: This loophole freed people from caring for their parents. A human rule had canceled out God’s clear command.

f.g: Made void, cancelled.

n: Jesus calls them hypocrites and says Isaiah described them perfectly long ago.

f.g: Esaias = Isaiah.

n: Quoting Isaiah: people honor God with their words while their hearts are far from him.

f.w: This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth

n: Worship becomes empty when human rules are taught as if they were God’s commandments.

f.g: Pointlessly, without effect.

n: Jesus now turns to the crowd with an important teaching.
What makes a person spiritually unclean isn’t food going in, but what comes out — words and actions flowing from the heart.

f.g: defile = make unclean, spiritually polluted.

f.w: that which cometh out of the mouth

n: The disciples warn Jesus that he has offended the Pharisees.

f.g: Greek skandalizō — caused to stumble, scandalized.

n: Teachings and leaders not rooted in God will eventually be pulled up like weeds.

f.w: Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted

n: Leave them be: they are blind guides leading blind followers, and both will end up in the pit.

f.g: A pit — perhaps an open well or cistern.

n: Peter asks Jesus to explain this saying, which he calls a parable.
Jesus is surprised that even his close disciples still don’t understand.
Food simply passes through the body; it doesn’t touch the heart.

f.g: draught = latrine, toilet.

n: Words and deeds, on the other hand, reveal and come from the heart.
Jesus lists the evils that begin in the heart. Notice that sinful actions start as sinful thoughts.

f.g: Sexual relations outside of marriage.

n: These are what truly make a person unclean before God — not eating with unwashed hands.

f.g: unwashen = unwashed.

n: Jesus travels northwest into Gentile territory near the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon.

f.g: coasts = region, borders.

n: A Gentile woman pleads with Jesus to free her tormented daughter. Surprisingly, she calls him “Son of David,” a title many in Israel wouldn’t use.

f.g: A Gentile; Mark calls her a Greek of Syrophenician birth. Canaanites were Israel’s ancient enemies.
Severely tormented.

n: At first Jesus says nothing. The disciples urge him to send her away because her pleading is embarrassing them.

f.w: he answered her not a word
f.g: His silence seems to test and draw out her faith.

n: Jesus explains that his mortal mission was first to Israel. The gospel would go to the Gentiles later.

f.w: the lost sheep of the house of Israel

n: Undeterred, she kneels before him and simply begs, “Lord, help me.”
Jesus uses a common saying: food for the children shouldn’t be given to the dogs. Israel had the first claim. His word for “dogs” is the softer word for household pets.

f.g: meet = right, fitting.
Greek kynaria — little dogs, house pets.

n: Her quick, humble answer accepts his words and finds hope in them: even pets get the crumbs that fall from the table.

f.g: Yes, Lord — that is true.

n: Jesus praises her great faith and heals her daughter at that moment. A Gentile woman becomes a model of persistent faith.
Returning to the Sea of Galilee, Jesus climbs a hillside and sits down to teach.

f.w: came nigh unto the sea of Galilee
f.g: Mark says through the Decapolis, the largely Gentile region east of the lake.

n: Huge crowds bring the disabled and sick and lay them at his feet, and he heals them.

f.g: maimed = crippled, missing or injured in a limb.

n: The people are amazed and praise “the God of Israel” — a phrase suggesting many of them were Gentiles.

f.w: they glorified the God of Israel

n: After three days with him, the people have no food. Jesus is concerned they’ll collapse on the way home.

f.g: Here simply: without food.

f.w: lest they faint in the way

n: The disciples wonder where they could find enough bread in such a remote place — even though they saw the 5,000 fed.

f.g: whence = from where.

n: They have seven loaves and a few small fish.

f.g: Seven often symbolizes completeness in scripture.

n: Jesus has the crowd sit down on the ground.
As before, Jesus gives thanks, breaks the bread, and has his disciples distribute it.

f.g: Greek eucharisteō — the root of “Eucharist.”

n: All eat their fill, and seven large baskets of leftovers are gathered.

f.g: meat = food; broken pieces of bread.
A different word than in 14:20 — large hampers, like the one Paul was later lowered in.

n: About 4,000 men, plus women and children, are fed — a second, separate miracle of abundance.
Jesus sends the crowd home and sails to Magdala on the western shore — likely the hometown of Mary Magdalene.

f.g: Some manuscripts read Magadan; Mark has Dalmanutha.
